The bainite ferrite laths are characterized by the carbides distributed along the lath boundaries.
When the tempering temperature was high up to 700◦C, small recrystallized grains appeared, as shown in Fig. 1e.
At the tempering temperature of 700 ◦C, the n value increased to n = 0.258.
Nevertheless, the tensile strength remarkably decreases to about 1000 MPa when tempered at 500◦C

Therefore, tempering at 500–650 ◦C can result in a depletion of the dissolved C and N atoms due to the precipitation of /H9255-carbides (FeC2) or carbonitrides, which might be responsible for the low strain-hardening exponent.
The steel samples tempered at 700 ◦C show “round roof” shaped tensile curves possessing high strain-hardening exponents due to the fine-grained microstructure in the as-recrystallized state.
The governing mechanism is the strong interactions of dislocations and interstitials with grain boundaries and the finely-dispersed precipitates of carbides and carbonitrides.
the newly formed, small, recrystallized grains not only increased the amount of grain boundaries, but also behaved as the second phase, resulting in high strain-hardening ability of this steel.
